legend.name: Water-filled sand
legend.meaning: Sand and gravel with every pore full of water

legend.name: Clay
legend.meaning: Tight layer that water barely passes through

steps.title: Ground
steps.instruction: Trace the ground surface on both sides of the well.

note.text: Below the ground, rock and sediment have tiny open spaces called pores. Groundwater is stored in them.

steps.title: Rain
steps.instruction: Draw the rain falling and the arrow soaking into the ground.

note.text: Rain and snowmelt soak into the ground and trickle down. This refills, or recharges, the groundwater.

steps.title: Saturated zone
steps.instruction: Trace the zone where every pore is full of water, on both sides.

note.text: Its top is the water table. Sand and gravel make a good aquifer: their pores are big and connected, so water flows through.
note.remember: Aquifer: rock that holds and passes water.

note.text: Clay's pores are tiny and poorly connected, so water barely moves through it. It holds the groundwater above it.

steps.title: Well
steps.instruction: Trace the well and its pump.

note.text: Pumping lowers the water around the well, making a dip in the water table: a cone of depression.
note.remember: Pumping draws the water table down.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the water-filled sand and the clay.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered part.

mistakes.Clay layer: This layer is sand and gravel that holds and passes water: the aquifer.

steps.title: Too much pumping
steps.question: A town pumps water out faster than rain can recharge the aquifer. What happens over the years?

options.text: The water table drops, and shallow wells can go dry
options.feedback: Yes. When the cone of depression spreads and deepens, nearby wells may end above the water and go dry.
Taking out more than comes in lowers the water, not raises it.
Groundwater is limited. It refills slowly, so heavy pumping can use it up.
The rock doesn't change. The water table drops.

steps.title: Uneven resources
steps.question: Why do some places have lots of groundwater and others very little?

options.text: It depends on the rock and sediment underground, which past geologic processes laid down
options.feedback: Right. Sand and gravel left by old rivers and glaciers hold lots of water; solid granite holds little.
It isn't. Porous sand and gravel hold far more than solid rock.
Groundwater collects naturally in porous rock and sediment.
Groundwater is found almost everywhere, but how much depends on the rock.
